title: Sound Practices for Responsible Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI): Final report
date_evidence: meta-article:published_time: 2026-10-15T04:00:01+00:00 (page shows: 15 October 2026 | PDF full text)
key_claim: The FSB's final report sets out 12 non-binding sound practices for responsible AI adoption by financial institutions; the human-oversight practice scales oversight to materiality, risk, autonomy, complexity and explainability.
frame_summary: The FSB frames human oversight of AI as something to be scaled to each use case's materiality and risk, not applied uniformly, within a set of practices institutions are encouraged to consider.
verbatim_quote: Financial institutions implement appropriate and effective human oversight relevant to the materiality, risk, autonomy, complexity, and explainability of different AI use cases.
verbatim_list: This report sets out 12 sound practices financial institutions are encouraged to consider to facilitate their responsible adoption of AI.
notes: Final report page, full text as displayed read via WebFetch 31/10/2026; PDF not fetched. Quotes confirmed against the page text.

title: Opening Remarks at Finance + A.I. Forum
key_claim: HKMA's Carmen Chu says effective oversight of agentic AI need not mean human involvement in every step but must mean clear accountability and on-going monitoring, and that guidance recognises a progressive shift from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop oversight.
frame_summary: The HKMA argues that agentic AI's autonomy calls for intent-anchored accountability and monitoring, which permits a shift from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop oversight rather than approval of every step.
verbatim_quote: As A.I. use cases become more sophisticated, effective oversight need not mean human involvement in every step.
verbatim_list: But it must mean clear accountability and on-going monitoring.
It also recognises a progressive shift from “human-in-the-loop” to “human-on-the-loop” oversight.
notes: Speech by Carmen Chu, Executive Director (Banking Supervision). Full page read via WebFetch 31/10/2026.

title: The Agentic Oversight Tax: Human Supervision of AI Agents Has a Cost that Must be Accounted For
date_evidence: Evergreen reference page, accessed 2026-10-31; no publication date on page; poster session shown as Sat, Dec 12, 2026
key_claim: A NeurIPS 2026 position paper argues human supervision of AI agents carries a measurable cognitive and organisational cost, and that governance frameworks mandating oversight without measuring that cost cannot verify the oversight is effective.
frame_summary: The paper argues that mandated human oversight of agents is only meaningful if its cost is measured, and proposes measurable components of that cost.
verbatim_quote: Governance frameworks mandating human oversight without measuring its cost cannot verify whether that oversight remains effective.
verbatim_list: This position paper argues that human supervision of AI agents imposes a composite cognitive, affective and organizational cost that no existing framework jointly captures.
notes: Abstract as displayed; position paper, author Olivier Oullier. Cited for the argument, not as measured evidence.

title: The State Of Agentic AI In 2026: Companies Are Chasing, Few Are Catching
key_claim: Forrester names a 'trust tax' on agentic AI: every autonomous action must be logged and defensible to an auditor, and the cost of that is currently too high.
frame_summary: Forrester argues enterprise governance has not kept pace with agent autonomy, and that the audit and logging burden is a cost that limits how far autonomy can widen.
verbatim_quote: Every autonomous action has to be logged and defensible to an auditor, and right now that cost is too high.
verbatim_list: Underneath all of it sits the trust tax.
notes: Structural anchor in the 3-6 month band (150 days). Cited for the trust-tax framing.

title: The share of enterprises trusting AI agents to make production changes on their own has fallen from 75% to 56%, VB Intelligence finds
key_claim: In VB Intelligence's August survey the purchaser share allowing or building toward unreviewed production changes by agents fell from 88% to 61%, and only 29% of agent deployers use real-time automated quality checks as the primary monitoring approach.
frame_summary: VentureBeat reports that enterprises are growing more cautious about letting automated evaluations authorise production changes without human review, while noting its respondents are self-selected.
verbatim_quote: Among final purchasing decision-makers whose organizations deploy autonomous agents, the share allowing unreviewed production changes or building toward them fell from 88% in July to 61% in August.
verbatim_list: This is a notable drop from 75% in VentureBeat’s July survey.

In VentureBeat’s August Agentic Reliability and Evaluations wave, 56% of respondents whose organizations deploy autonomous AI agents said they already allow certain production changes based on automated evaluation results alone, without human review, or are engineering their systems to permit this within the next year.

Among the 118 August respondents whose organizations deploy autonomous agents, only 29% said their primary production monitoring approach uses real-time automated quality checks on live agent outputs.
More than half (53%) of August's 140 respondents were final AI purchasing decision-makers, compared with 44% in July.
notes: Vendor-run reader survey with self-selected respondents (the page says so); used directionally.

title: New G2 Research: AI Agents Have Moved From Pilot to Production. Now Comes the Distrust Tax.
key_claim: G2's survey of B2B software buyers finds 45% say overseeing and correcting agent mistakes consumes more than a quarter of expected productivity gains, 52% require human quality review before production, and 4 in 5 teams in mature workflows report cycle-time gains of at least 11%.
frame_summary: G2 argues agents have reached production but oversight of agents buyers do not fully trust carries a 'distrust tax' that erodes returns.
verbatim_quote: 45% say time spent overseeing and correcting agent mistakes consumes more than a quarter of the productivity gains they expected, and 46% report higher-than-expected operating costs.
verbatim_list: 52% require human quality review before production, and 77% re-evaluate agent performance at least monthly.
Among teams running agents in mature workflows, 4 in 5 report cycle-time gains of at least 11%.
notes: Software-review vendor survey of more than 1,000 buyers; blog post only, full report not fetched.

title: IBM Study: Eight in Ten EMEA Enterprises Escalate AI Incidents to Board or C-Suite as AI Agents Test Governance
key_claim: IBM's EMEA study finds 75% of executives expect AI agents to have some autonomy over decisions by 2027 but only 37% say their governance is designed to scale with agentic AI.
frame_summary: IBM argues that incidents are reaching boards in Europe and the Middle East while governance, accountability and risk quantification lag behind agent adoption.
verbatim_quote: 75% of respondents expect AI agents to have some level of autonomy with respect to decisions by 2027, yet only 37% say their governance is designed to scale with agentic AI deployment.
notes: Vendor-commissioned survey (Censuswide, 3,221 executives). Page date Oct 14, body dateline Oct 15; the visible header date is used.
